# Conventions {.unnumbered}

This book uses a small set of visual conventions, and uses
them the same way in every chapter.

## Where you are

Each chapter opens with the same diagram of a reproducible
analysis, with the stage the chapter teaches highlighted. The
six stages along the top follow the order of work. The two bands
beneath them apply to all six stages.




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The analysis pipeline that opens each chapter. Here the Wrangle stage is highlighted, as it is in the wrangling chapter.](conventions_files/figure-pdf/fig-conventions-pipeline-1.pdf){#fig-conventions-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Wrangle.' width=100%}
:::
:::


## In code blocks

- Input lines carry no prefix.
- Output lines are prefixed with `#>`. The whole block stays a
  valid R script: paste it into a console and it runs without
  error.
- Numbered discs in the code gutter (1, 2, 3) are annotations.
  Hover or tap them to read the annotation, or read the
  numbered list below the block.
- Code shown but not run, such as shell commands that would
  change your machine, is said to be display-only where it
  appears.

A minimal example:

```{.r}
library(dplyr)

penguins |>                                       # <1>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |>                  # <2>
  group_by(species) |>                            # <3>
  summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g))
```
1. Start the pipeline with the `penguins` data frame.
2. Drop rows with missing body-mass values.
3. Compute the species-level mean body mass.

## In prose

- **Bold** marks a term on its first use; the glossary in the
  appendix defines it.
- `monospace` marks code, file paths, and package names.
- `package::function()` disambiguates function ownership when
  the package is not obvious from context.
- Asides, history, and version notes are footnotes. They are
  shown in the margin of the web edition and at the foot of the
  page in print, so that the main text carries only what you
  need.
- 'Habit 6' and similar refer to the numbered habits in
  @sec-habits.

## Callouts

The book uses five kinds, so that each one means one thing.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
A short question after a major section, with its answer
folded inside. Try it before you open it: recalling an answer
before reading it helps you retain the idea.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
A command to run after a worked example that confirms it did
what it claims. If the check fails, stop and find out why
before going on.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
A silent failure that analysts meet in practice: code that
runs without error and produces a wrong answer.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A prompt for a language model or coding agent, placed beside
the task it helps with, with the check that verifies what it
returns. Send models structure, not data; @sec-ai-governance
says why.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title='Ethics'}
A short flag where a technical step can harm the people in the
data or mislead a reader, pointing to the fuller treatment in
@sec-ethics.
:::

Exercise solutions sit in folded blocks titled 'Solution'
directly beneath each exercise. The printed edition cannot fold
blocks. There, Check answers and solutions are collected at the
end of each chapter instead, so that you can attempt a question
before you see its answer.
